## The big idea

Run the ledger backward. A pump buys angular momentum for the fluid; a
turbine sells it — same Euler equation, opposite sign, and the same
specific-speed sorting hat deciding the machine's shape. Two strategies
exist for the extraction. **Impulse** machines (Pelton) first cash the
entire head into one screaming jet, then mug it with buckets. **Reaction**
machines (Francis, Kaplan) let the pressure drop *through* the spinning
runner itself, gaining a trick the impulse wheel can't use: a draft tube
that keeps recovering energy after the runner is done. Between them — plus
one windmill theorem you already proved — they power about a sixth of the
planet.

::: {.callout-note}
### The number in charge: the speed ratio $U/V$
For a Pelton wheel, bucket speed over jet speed. Power is zero at $U = 0$
(all force, no motion) and zero at $U = V$ (the buckets outrun the water) —
and the maximum sits exactly at $U/V = 1/2$. One dimensionless knob, one
best answer, and every alpine powerhouse is tuned to it.
:::

## The impulse strategy: Pelton

An alpine penstock delivers head $H$ to a nozzle; Torricelli hands back a
jet at $V = \sqrt{2gH}$ (Unit 4, still undefeated). The wheel's buckets —
split spoons, really — catch the jet and turn it nearly $180°$.

Momentum accounting in the bucket's frame (Unit 5, verbatim): water arrives
at $V - U$, leaves reversed, so each unit of mass gives up close to
$2(V-U)$ of velocity change. Here is the assumption that separates the
wheel from the lone cart: the buckets parade past the nozzle in close
order, so the jet never travels extra distance to catch its target — **the
full $\dot m = \rho Q$ is always being worked on**, regardless of $U$.
Force $\approx 2\rho Q (V-U)$, and power is force times bucket speed:

$$P(U) \;\approx\; 2\rho Q\,(V - U)\,U.$$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Click for the optimum (and the cart comparison)
$dP/dU = 2\rho Q (V - 2U) = 0 \Rightarrow U = V/2$, with
$P_\text{max} = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho Q V^2$ — the jet's *entire* kinetic power.
The lone cart of CT-5-5 lives by different rules: retreating at $U$, it
meets a diminished mass flow $\rho A (V-U)$, so $P \propto (V-U)^2 U$,
peaking at $U = V/3$ and capturing at best $\tfrac{8}{27}$ of… a moving
target. One assumption about $\dot m$, two different optima. Check which
world your problem lives in before quoting a magic fraction.
:::

At $U = V/2$ with a perfect $180°$ turn, the water leaves the bucket at
$-(V-U) + U = 0$ in the ground frame: it **dribbles off the wheel dead**,
its kinetic energy handed over in full. That morgue-quiet exit is the whole
design goal — energy still moving is energy not sold — and it's why real
Pelton wheels post efficiencies in the low 90s.[^angle] Impulse machines run
at atmospheric pressure around the runner, so all the head must be converted
in the nozzle first: they are the natural choice when $H$ is enormous and
$Q$ is modest. The specific-speed sorting hat agrees: tiny $N_s$, impulse
country.

[^angle]: Real buckets turn the flow ~$165°$, not $180°$ — the water must
exit sideways enough to miss the back of the next bucket. Physics charges a
few percent for the clearance.

## The reaction strategy: Francis & Kaplan

Now let the pressure drop happen *inside* the machine. In a reaction
turbine the runner runs full and pressurized; guide vanes set the swirl,
the runner un-swirls the flow and pockets the angular momentum (Euler,
sign flipped). Two consequences worth owning.

First, the habitat: Francis runners (the workhorses — think Hoover Dam)
take medium heads at serious flows; Kaplan machines are axial propellers
with adjustable pitch, built for run-of-river duties where the head might
be a polite 4 m but the flow is a county's worth of water. It is the pump
story mirrored: as $N_s$ climbs, the machine stretches from radial to
axial. `select_machine()` will referee.

Second, the exit. Water leaves a runner still carrying velocity head
$U^2/2g$ — several meters' worth in a big unit. The **draft tube** — a
gently flaring diffuser between runner and tailrace — slows that flow and
converts the recovered head into *lower pressure at the runner exit*,
which the turbine harvests as extra working head. It is the venturi
recovery argument of module 4.2 rerun for profit.[^cav] Impulse wheels,
spinning in air, get no such refund; it's the reaction family's structural
advantage at low head, where the exit KE would otherwise be a painful
fraction of the whole budget.

[^cav]: The refund has a price: the draft tube *lowers* the pressure at the
runner exit — so cavitation stalks turbines at the **outlet**, the mirror
image of the pump's inlet problem. Same physics as module 8.4, same vapor
pressure, new address. Setting the runner low enough relative to the
tailwater is the turbine's NPSH story.

And the machine with no casing at all — the wind turbine — answers to the
ceiling you derived in module 5.3: no shroudless rotor beats Betz's
$16/27$, because the air must leave with enough kinetic energy to clear
the scene. Clever blades negotiate *toward* the limit, never past it.

## Play with it

A mountain penstock ($H$, $Q$ below) feeds one nozzle. Compare the bucket
parade against the lone cart as you sweep the speed ratio — same jet, two
mass-flow assumptions.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof H_103 = Inputs.range([100, 800], {value: 400, step: 25, label: "gross head H (m)"})
viewof Q_103 = Inputs.range([0.05, 0.6], {value: 0.2, step: 0.05, label: "flow Q (m³/s)"})
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|   - H_103
#|   - Q_103
rho = 998.2
V = np.sqrt(2*9.81*H_103)
r = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)          # U/V
P_wheel = 2*rho*Q_103*(V - r*V)*(r*V) / 1e6      # bucket parade, MW
P_cart  = rho*Q_103*(V - r*V)**2*(r*V)/V / 1e6   # lone cart: ṁ shrinks with (V-U)/V
P_jet   = 0.5*rho*Q_103*V**2 / 1e6

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.6))
ax.plot(r, P_wheel, lw=2.5, color='crimson', label='Pelton wheel (full ṁ always)')
ax.plot(r, P_cart, lw=2.5, color='steelblue', ls='--', label='single runaway cart (ṁ shrinks)')
ax.axhline(P_jet, color='gray', lw=1, ls=':')
ax.annotate(f' jet power {P_jet:.2f} MW', (0.02, P_jet*0.99), fontsize=9,
            color='gray', va='top')
ax.plot(0.5, max(P_wheel), 'o', ms=11, mfc='gold', mec='k', zorder=5)
ax.annotate(f"  U/V = 1/2: {max(P_wheel):.2f} MW\n  (jet speed V = {V:.0f} m/s)",
            (0.5, max(P_wheel)), fontsize=9, va='top')
ax.plot(1/3, max(P_cart), 's', ms=9, mfc='white', mec='steelblue', zorder=5)
ax.annotate(" U/V = 1/3", (1/3, max(P_cart)), fontsize=9, color='steelblue', va='bottom')
ax.set_xlabel('speed ratio U/V'); ax.set_ylabel('power (MW)')
ax.set_title("two optima, one assumption apart — and the wheel banks the whole jet")
ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.set_ylim(0, P_jet*1.12)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Three experiments. **Confirm the endpoints**: both curves die at $U/V = 0$
and $1$ — force without motion, motion without force; power insists on
both. **Read the gap** between the crimson peak and the gray line: the
ideal wheel at $U = V/2$ collects the *entire* jet power (the water leaves
dead), while the cart tops out at $8/27$ of a number that isn't even fixed.
**Crank the head** and watch the stakes: at 800 m the jet arrives at
$125$ m/s — the buckets are being sandblasted by water moving at a
respectable fraction of highway-aircraft speed, which is why Pelton runners
are solid stainless forgings and not enthusiasm.

::: {.callout-important}
## The misconception to leave behind
"Faster buckets catch more energy — run the wheel as fast as it will spin."
At $U = V$ the buckets *never touch the water*: zero force, zero power, and
an overspeeding wheel to boot. Extraction is a negotiation: slow enough to
be hit hard, fast enough to carry the work away. The optimum is a
compromise — in this course, it always is (Betz's $1/3$, the cart's $V/3$,
the wheel's $V/2$: three flavors of the same bargain).
:::

## Check yourself

<details><summary>**Q1.** An alpine site offers 600 m of head and 0.3 m³/s; a run-of-river site offers 5 m and 80 m³/s. Assign the machines, and name the number that did the assigning.</summary>
Specific speed. The alpine duty (huge $H$, small $Q$) drives $N_s$ down —
impulse/Pelton territory. The river (tiny $H$, huge $Q$) drives it up —
axial/Kaplan. Comparable *powers*, wildly different shapes: the duty chose,
the number announced it, the engineer obeyed.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q2.** Standing below a running Pelton wheel, the discharge water falls almost straight down into the tailrace. Diagnose the machine's health from that one observation.</summary>
Healthy — very. Water leaving with no horizontal velocity has handed over
essentially all its kinetic energy: the wheel is running near $U = V/2$.
Discharge water still moving briskly downstream would be revenue walking
out the door (and a speed ratio off its mark).
</details>

<details><summary>**Q3.** A Kaplan turbine's draft tube is flared at ~8°, never 30°. Why flare at all, and why not more? (Both answers live in earlier units.)</summary>
Flaring diffuses the exit flow, recovering velocity head as reduced runner
back-pressure — the venturi-recovery logic of module 4.2, worth real meters
on a low-head plant. But diffusers past ~8–10° separate (Unit 7's adverse-
gradient story), and a stalled draft tube recovers nothing while shaking
the powerhouse. The angle is a truce between recovery and separation.
</details>
